title: GoodRx shared prescription data for advertising
hook: A drug-discount app told Facebook which medications people bought.
collected: Prescription medications, health conditions and contact details of people using GoodRx's discount app and website.
howObtained: Users gave it to get drug coupons. It then flowed out through tracking code from Facebook, Google, Criteo and others built into the app and site.
inferred: Health conditions, from which medications a person bought or searched for.
done: The FTC alleged GoodRx shared this data with advertising platforms and, in 2019, uploaded lists of users who bought particular medications to Facebook so it could target them with health-related ads. It also alleged a misleading HIPAA seal.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC complaint resolved by a court order. GoodRx did not admit wrongdoing.

companyResponse.text: GoodRx said it does not agree with the FTC's allegations, admits no wrongdoing, and settled to avoid the cost of litigation.
companyResponse.source: GoodRx statement, as reported in search results (original page blocked)

outcome.text: $1.5 million civil penalty and a permanent ban on sharing health data for advertising. The FTC called it its first enforcement of the Health Breach Notification Rule.

sources.title: FTC Enforcement Action to Bar GoodRx from Sharing Consumers' Sensitive Health Info for Advertising
FTC slaps online pharmacy GoodRx for sharing users' health data

limits: The penalty is small next to the company's revenue, and the facts come from the FTC's complaint rather than a trial.
whyItMatters: A coupon app is not a doctor, so US medical-privacy law (HIPAA) did not protect this data the way people assumed.

title: BetterHelp shared therapy sign-up answers with ad platforms
hook: People seeking therapy answered intake questions; the answers fed advertising.
collected: Email addresses, IP addresses and answers to an intake questionnaire, including whether someone had been in therapy before.
howObtained: Users filled in the questionnaire to be matched with a counsellor.
inferred: That a person was seeking mental-health help.
done: The FTC alleged BetterHelp shared this information with Facebook, Snapchat, Criteo and Pinterest for advertising, despite promising privacy, and in 2020 falsely denied press reports about it.
affected: People who paid for BetterHelp between August 2017 and December 2020; about 800,000 were later sent refund notices.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC order. BetterHelp did not admit wrongdoing.

companyResponse.text: BetterHelp says the settlement is not an admission of wrongdoing, and describes the practices as industry-standard.

outcome.text: $7.8 million for partial refunds and a ban on sharing health data for advertising. Refund notices went to about 800,000 customers in 2024.

sources.title: FTC to Ban BetterHelp from Revealing Consumers' Data, Including Sensitive Mental Health Information, to Facebook and Others
BetterHelp response to the recent FTC settlement
BetterHelp customers to receive refunds over data misuse

limits: Refunds were small (around $10 each per reports). The facts are the FTC's allegations, settled, not tried.
whyItMatters: The moment someone looks for help is one of the most sensitive moments there is.

title: Flo period-tracking app shared health data through software kits
hook: A period tracker promised privacy, then passed pregnancy and cycle data to analytics firms.
collected: Menstrual cycle and pregnancy information that users logged in the Flo app (more than 100 million users).
howObtained: Users entered it themselves to track their cycles.
done: The FTC alleged that, despite privacy promises, Flo shared this data with Facebook, Google, AppsFlyer and Flurry through software development kits (SDKs) built into the app, until a Wall Street Journal story in February 2019.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC order (5-0 vote). No admission of wrongdoing.

outcome.text: Final order requiring user consent, notice to users and that recipients delete data. No money.

sources.title: Developer of Popular Women's Fertility-Tracking App Settles FTC Allegations

limits: The FTC order carried no money; two commissioners argued it should have been brought as a health-breach case.
whyItMatters: SDKs are code from other companies inside an app. Users cannot see them, and the app maker may not fully control what they send.

title: Jury finds Meta liable over Flo app data
hook: In a class action, a jury decided Meta's tracking in a period app broke California's wiretap law.
collected: Data from Flo app users sent to Meta through its software kit.
howObtained: Meta's SDK embedded in the Flo app.
inferred: Reproductive health information, according to plaintiffs.
done: A federal jury in Frasco v. Flo Health found Meta liable under the California Invasion of Privacy Act. Google, Flo and Flurry settled before the verdict for a combined $59.5 million.
affected: A class of Flo users (reported as tens of millions).
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Jury verdict. Damages had not been set as of November 2026; further appeals are possible.

companyResponse.text: Meta said it disagreed with the verdict and would explore all legal options.

outcome.text: Meta's post-trial motions were denied (September 2025, per secondary reports). A damages decision was still pending as of November 2026.

sources.title: Frasco v. Flo Health, Inc. case page
Jury Finds Meta Liable for Misusing Women's Health Data

limits: The case page belongs to the plaintiffs' lawyers. The final damages and any appeal outcome are unknown.
whyItMatters: A rare case where ordinary people, not a regulator, won a verdict over a tracking SDK.

title: Meta Pixel on hospital websites
hook: Booking a doctor's appointment online could send details to Facebook.
collected: Clicks on 'schedule appointment' buttons, doctors' names, search terms such as 'pregnancy termination' and, inside some patient portals, medications and allergies.
howObtained: The Meta Pixel, a snippet of tracking code that hospitals had added to their own websites.
inferred: Possible health conditions linked to a browser or Facebook account.
done: The Markup tested the top 100 US hospitals and found the pixel sending such data to Meta on 33 of their websites, and inside 7 patient portals.
label: REPORTED
labelNote: Investigative journalism with a published, reproducible technical method. Class-action claims about it are ALLEGED.

companyResponse.text: Meta said that sensitive data its systems detect "will be removed before it can be stored in our ads systems".
companyResponse.source: Meta spokesperson quoted by The Markup

outcome.text: Many hospitals removed the pixel after the report; at least 35 of 40 systems later contacted had done so. Lawsuits followed.

sources.title: Facebook Is Receiving Sensitive Medical Information from Hospital Websites
Meta Faces Mounting Questions from Congress

limits: Shows data was sent, not what Meta did with it afterwards.
whyItMatters: Third-party code on websites you trust is invisible to you, and sometimes to the site owner too.

title: Data brokers offered to sell mental-health data
hook: A researcher asked 37 data brokers for lists of people with depression and anxiety. Eleven said yes.
collected: Data about Americans' mental-health conditions, such as depression, anxiety, ADHD, bipolar disorder, insomnia and PTSD.
howObtained: Brokers assemble it from many sources; the report did not trace every origin.
done: Researcher Joanne Kim contacted 37 brokers; 26 responded and 11 were willing to sell mental-health data. One quoted $275 for 5,000 aggregated counts; others offered subscriptions of $75,000 to $100,000 a year.
affected: Americans whose data is held by brokers.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: A university research report describing its method (Duke Sanford School).

outcome.text: No enforcement action tied to the report.

sources.title: Data Brokers and the Sale of Americans' Mental Health Data
sources.publisher: Duke Sanford School of Public Policy

sources.title: Study finds data brokers selling Americans' mental health data

limits: The researcher did not complete large purchases, so the quality of what was offered is unknown.
whyItMatters: You can buy this kind of data without being a doctor, insurer or employer.

title: Mozilla's review of mental-health apps
hook: Most prayer, therapy and mood apps reviewed got a privacy warning label.
collected: Varies by app: moods, journal entries, chats with counsellors or bots, device data.
howObtained: Users enter it in the apps.
done: Mozilla's *Privacy Not Included team reviewed 32 mental-health apps; in 2023, 19 of 32 still earned its privacy warning label. It reported one app (Cerebral) loading 799 trackers in the first minute.
label: REPORTED
labelNote: Independent NGO review of privacy policies and app behaviour, with a described method. Not a regulator finding.

outcome.text: Some apps improved policies between 2022 and 2023, according to Mozilla.

sources.title: Shady Mental Health Apps Inch Toward Privacy and Security Improvements

limits: Mozilla's 2022 baseline figures are reported inconsistently across its own pages. A warning label reflects policy and practice concerns, not proof of misuse.
whyItMatters: Reading a privacy policy is hard; independent reviewers do it for you.
